items.title: Mendeleev predicted germanium 15 years before anyone made it
items.claim: In 1871 Mendeleev published predicted properties for an undiscovered element he called 'eka-silicon'. In 1886 Winkler isolated germanium. The predicted atomic mass was 72; measured 72.6. Predicted density 5.5 g/cm3; measured 5.32.
items.prompt: How could Mendeleev predict an unknown element?

options.text: He used patterns in the existing table: rows and columns of known elements bracketed each gap. An element in the silicon column, between gallium and arsenic, must have intermediate properties — and atomic mass close to the average of its neighbours
He had advance information from chemists in Germany

items.reveal:
Mendeleev's 1871 predicted properties for eka-silicon: atomic mass ~72, density ~5.5 g/cm3, grey metal, oxide formula MO2 with density ~4.7 g/cm3, chloride MCl4 boiling under 100°C.

Winkler's 1886 germanium: atomic mass 72.6, density 5.32 g/cm3, grey metal, GeO2 density 4.7 g/cm3, GeCl4 boiling at 86°C.

The match converted scepticism into acceptance. The periodic table stopped being a memorisation aid and became a predictive theory. Similar predictions held for gallium (eka-aluminium, 1875) and scandium (eka-boron, 1879).

The predictions could not have worked if the table were merely an empirical classification. The fact that it predicted real properties of unknown elements showed that something deeper was being captured.
items.why: Theories earn their keep by predicting what no one has measured yet. Mendeleev's table did this three times in 17 years.

items.title: Hafnium and zirconium are almost impossible to tell apart
items.claim: Zirconium and hafnium sit one above the other in Group 4 — separated by the entire lanthanide row. They have almost identical atomic radii (160 vs 159 pm), nearly identical ionic radii, and remarkably similar chemistry.
items.prompt: Why doesn't hafnium have a larger radius like the down-group trend predicts?

options.text: Hafnium has fewer electrons than expected

The 14 lanthanide elements between them add 14 protons but the 4f electrons screen the nucleus very poorly, so the effective nuclear charge experienced by the 5d and 6s shells in Hf is much higher than down-group trends suggest — the 'lanthanide contraction'
Hafnium atoms are crushed by gravity

items.reveal:
Across the 14 lanthanides, atomic number rises by 14 but the added electrons go into 4f orbitals 'inside' the 6s shell. Because 4f electrons screen poorly, the outer electrons see steadily more effective nuclear charge — and the atomic radius shrinks across the row.

By the time you reach hafnium (Z=72), the radius is essentially the same as zirconium (Z=40, four periods up the table). The two elements are chemically near-identical and have to be separated by very fine techniques — typically ion exchange chromatography.

Nuclear reactor design depends on the separation. Zirconium is used for fuel-rod cladding (very low neutron absorption); hafnium has a neutron cross-section about 600 times higher and is used for control rods. Mixing them up is catastrophic.
items.why: Down-group similarity is taught; lateral similarity caused by f-shell shielding is a hidden consequence of the full periodic table.

items.title: The endpoint of a titration is NOT the equivalence point
items.claim: Titrate vinegar with sodium hydroxide using phenolphthalein. The colour changes when you've added enough base — that's the endpoint. Strictly, the equivalence point (exactly stoichiometric) and the endpoint (when the indicator changes) are two different things.
items.prompt: Why use phenolphthalein with weak-acid + strong-base titrations?

options.text: Its colour change at pH 8.2-10.0 matches the steep pH jump that occurs near the equivalence point in a weak-acid + strong-base titration; choosing the right indicator makes endpoint approximately equal to equivalence point

items.reveal:
A titration of ethanoic acid (pKa 4.76) with NaOH has equivalence point pH around 8.7 (not 7! — the conjugate base CH3COO- is itself basic). Phenolphthalein, with its colour change between pH 8.2 and 10, brackets this.

Methyl orange (pH 3.1-4.4) would change colour FAR before the equivalence point and give a wrong result for the acid concentration.

A strong acid + strong base titration has equivalence at pH 7 with a very steep pH jump — almost any indicator works. A weak acid + weak base titration has no sharp pH jump at all and is usually monitored with a pH meter, not an indicator.
items.why: Titrations are presented as if indicator change marks the answer exactly. The match between indicator pKa and equivalence pH determines accuracy.
